{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Stanley Ernest Whitcomb''' (born January 23, 1951, in [[Denver]])<ref>biographical information according to ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> is an American physicist and was the chief scientist at the [[LIGO|Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO)]] project when the first direct detection of [[gravitational wave]]s was made in September 2015.<ref>{{cite web|title=Whitcomb, Stanley E. Interview by Heidi Aspaturian. Pasadena, California, April 24, May 8 and 22, June 5 and 19, 2017|website=Oral History Project, California Institute of Technology|url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechOH:OH_Whitcomb_S_Ligo_2017}}</ref>

==Education and career==
In 1973 Whitcomb graduated with a bachelor's degree physics from [[Caltech]]. After a year at the [[University of Cambridge]], he became a physics graduate student at the [[University of Chicago]], where he graduated with a Ph.D. in 1980. His dissertation, supervised by Roger Hildebrand, dealt with astronomy in the far infrared and sub-millimeter wavelengths. In the autumn of 1980 Whitcomb became an assistant professor at Caltech.<ref name=IsaacsonAward>{{cite web|title=2019 Richard A. Isaacson Award in Gravitational-Wave Science Recipient, Stanley E. Whitcomb, LIGO Laboratory|website=APS Physics|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Whitcomb&first_nm=Stanley&year=2019}}</ref>

{{blockquote|Whitcomb joined the gravitational wave effort in 1980 and participated in the early experimental work that proved the feasibility of making such precise measurements. He led the team within the LIGO Laboratory that designed and commissioned the first generation full-scale LIGO detectors. At one point or another, he was involved in virtually every aspect of LIGO’s work.<ref name=DraperMedal>{{cite web|title=2017 Henry Draper Medal|url=http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/2017/Barish-Whitcomb.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170131050627/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/2017/Barish-Whitcomb.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 31, 2017|website=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref>}}

[[Kip Thorne]] and [[Ronald Drever]] were the earliest leaders of Caltech's pioneering gravitational wave program. Whitcomb, [[Siu Au Lee]], Robert E. Spero, and Mark Hereld were among the program's first five recruits. In 1985 Whitcomb moved to Northrop Corporation as a research engineer in the electronics division and then became a project manager. From 1989 to 1991 he was a senior system specialist at Loral Electro-Optical Systems. In 1991 he returned to LIGO as deputy director under Director [[Rochus Eugen Vogt|Rochus "Robbie" Vogt]], who in 1987 had taken charge of the joint LIGO Project between MIT (where [[Rainer Weiss]] worked on laser interferometers) and Caltech.<ref>{{cite web|title=Whitcomb, Stanley. Interview by Shirley K. Cohen. Pasadena, California, March 7 and 14, 1997|website=Oral History Project, California Institute of Technology Archives|url=http://oralhistories.library.caltech.edu/240/}}</ref> In September 2015 Whitcomb officially retired from LIGO but continued to make various contributions to the project.<ref name=MeesMedal>{{cite web|title=C.E.K. Mees Medal awarded to Stanley Whitcomb|website=LIGO news|date=August 20, 2018|url=https://www.ligo.caltech.edu/news/ligo20180820}}</ref>

In 2002 Whitcomb was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS).<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=APS Physics|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2002&unit_id=&institution=California+Institute+of+Technology}}</ref> He was elected a Fellow of [[The Optical Society]] in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|title=Stanley E. Whitcomb|website=OSA Living History|url=https://www.osa.org/en-us/history/biographies/bios/stanley_e_whitcomb/}}</ref> He has received several awards.<ref name=MeesMedal/><ref name=IsaacsonAward/> He received, jointly with [[Barry Barish]], the [[Henry Draper Medal]] in 2017.<ref name=DraperMedal/> In 2019, he received OSA's C.E.K. Mees Medal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smith |first=Meredith |last2=Apter |first2=Kari |last3=Gass |first3=Jeanette |date=2018-06-01 |title=2018 OSA Awards and Medals |url=https://opg.optica.org/opn/abstract.cfm?uri=opn-29-6-41 |journal=Optics and Photonics News |language=EN |volume=29 |issue=6 |pages=41–51 |doi=10.1364/OPN.29.6.000041 |issn=1541-3721|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
